Name: Logging Atlas Cedar and the Keels of Mediterranean Warships
RagShortTexts: The tall, tough North African cedar of the Atlas Mountains was the finest raw material for shipbuilding keels
The wood is rich in natural preservative oils, resists seawater and withstands the impact of Roman rams
Hannibal and the Carthaginian dockyards secretly relied on inland Berber tribes to fell and ship the timber
BaseText: Command of the sea in the classical age was in essence a military-industrial contest for fine forest resources. A quinquereme, through high-speed ramming and soaking in seawater, made extreme demands on the toughness, straightness and corrosion resistance of its keel timber. Carthage's key trump card in shipbuilding was rooted in the vast primeval forests above two thousand meters in the Atlas Mountains of North Africa: the 'North African Atlas cedar' (Cedrus atlantica). This tree has an extremely straight trunk, a single tree can reach forty meters in height, its wood is dense and tough, and it is naturally rich in fragrant preservative resin, so that it can soak in salty seawater for decades without shipworm and can absorb violent impact forces without easily cracking or snapping. Through privileged alliances with the inland Berber mountain tribes, Carthage organized thousands of slave loggers to fell the giant trees in the spring thaw and float them out of the mountains on the swollen spring waters of the Bagradas River. This became the strategic foundation that let the Punic navy quickly rise again and rebuild its fleets after several disasters at sea.

Variants.Content: Stroking the hard red keel of Atlas cedar is like touching the spine of the sea god! As long as the snow lies on the high peaks of the Atlas, Carthage's black-lacquered keels can smash the prow of any enemy ship!

We fell towering trees on snow-covered mountains, and the Carthaginian merchants take them away in exchange for bronze mirrors and coarse sackcloth. The great trees of the mountain forests grow fewer and fewer, while the fires of war below burn ever hotter.

The oaks and larches of the Italian Apennines made Rome's thick, unbreakable hulls. When the great ships of the two powers ram each other on the sea, it is really a duel to the death between Gallic oak and Atlas cedar!
